As public opinion has quickly soured over the summer on the facilities — which house energy-consuming, noise-producing, water-guzzling infrastructure for artificial intelligence programs — many politicians on both the left and right have increasingly signaled new skepticism about them. Cities and states, red and blue alike, have swiftly enacted fresh regulations to conserve environmental resources from data centers' impacts while moving to shield consumers' electricity bills from spiking because of them, too.

Data-center proponents argue there are major benefits to them, though. Trade unions have stressed they create blue-collar jobs. Democrats and Republicans have professed a need for the United States to stay at the frontier of emerging AI technology, underlining what they see are the critical national security implications of doing so. Maintaining a competitive edge against China is also a big part of the debate.

One of the most illustrative examples of how the public debate over data centers has changed this year is in Pennsylvania.

Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat who's running for reelection and is also an expected 2028 presidential contender, has significantly shifted his tone on the issue. Just over a year ago, he publicly touted Amazon's decision to build data centers in his state, saying the choice proved his administration could "work at the speed of business." He lauded the anticipated economic growth, including an influx of jobs.
This month, however, he signed an executive order slapping more regulations on big-tech companies and developers, saying Pennsylvanians wouldn't be "bullied" by hot-shot Silicon Valley lawyers.

Other Democrats, including Bobby Pulido, who's running against Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz to flip Texas' 15th Congressional District, are now arguing the job-growth argument has been overstated.
“Those data centers don't provide a lot of jobs other than building them," he told USA TODAY earlier this summer. "But that's it. That's a one-shot, one-time deal."
